claim: Type V CRISPR-Cas interference proteins use a single RuvC active site to make RNA-guided breaks in double-stranded DNA substrates.
source: Type V CRISPR-Cas interference proteins use a single RuvC active site to make RNA-guided breaks in double-stranded DNA substrates, an activity essential for both bacterial immunity and genome editing.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of Type V CRISPR-Cas proteins.

claim: Cas12a initiates DNA cutting by forming a 20-nucleotide R-loop in which the guide RNA displaces one strand of a double-helical DNA substrate.
source: The best-studied of these enzymes, Cas12a, initiates DNA cutting by forming a 20-nucleotide R-loop in which the guide RNA displaces one strand of a double-helical DNA substrate, positioning the DNase active site for first-strand cleavage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established mechanism of Cas12a action.

claim: DNA flanking the RNA-3′ side of R-loops exhibits intrinsic instability.
source: Here, we detect intrinsic instability in DNA flanking the RNA-3′ side of R-loops, which Cas12a can exploit to expose second-strand DNA for cutting.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: DNA flanking the RNA-5′ side of R-loops is not intrinsically unstable.
source: Interestingly, DNA flanking the RNA-5′ side of R-loops is not intrinsically unstable.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data comparing Cas12a and Cas9 R-loop structures.

claim: Cas12a can exploit R-loop flank instability to expose second-strand DNA for cutting.
source: Here, we detect intrinsic instability in DNA flanking the RNA-3′ side of R-loops, which Cas12a can exploit to expose second-strand DNA for cutting.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation stated in the abstract and supported by permanganate reactivity and cleavage site distribution experiments.

claim: Asymmetry in R-loop structure may explain the uniformity of guide RNA architecture in type V CRISPR-Cas systems.
source: This asymmetry in R-loop structure may explain the uniformity of guide RNA architecture and the single-active-site cleavage mechanism that are fundamental features of all type V CRISPR-Cas systems.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion stated in the abstract based on the observed asymmetry in R-loop flank stability.

claim: Both Cas9 and Cas12a use CRISPR RNA (crRNA) to recognize matching double-stranded DNA sequences by forming an R-loop structure in which 20 nucleotides of the crRNA base pair with one strand of the target DNA.
source: Both Cas9 and Cas12a use CRISPR RNA (crRNA) to recognize matching double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) sequences by forming an R-loop structure in which 20 nucleotides (nts) of the crRNA (the crRNA 'spacer') base pair with one strand of the target DNA (Figure 1A,B; Jinek et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2016; Zetsche et al., 2015; Swarts et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations to previous literature.

claim: Both Cas9 and Cas12a must bind to a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) to initiate R-loop formation.
source: In addition, both protein families must bind to a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM), a short DNA sequence next to the crRNA-complementary sequence, to initiate R-loop formation (Bolotin et al., 2005; Mojica et al., 2009; Sternberg et al., 2014; Singh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations to previous literature.

claim: Cas9 employs two active sites to generate a blunt DNA double-strand break near the PAM.
source: Cas9 employs two active sites to generate a blunt DNA double-strand break near the PAM (Jinek et al., 2012; Gasiunas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations to previous literature.

claim: Cas12a uses a single active site to make staggered cuts distant from the PAM.
source: In contrast, Cas12a uses a single active site to make staggered cuts distant from the PAM, and the same active site can cleave free single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) non-specifically once the enzyme has been activated by specific target binding (Figure 1B; Zetsche et al., 2015; Swarts et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations to previous literature.

claim: Cas12a can cleave free single-stranded DNA non-specifically once activated by specific target binding.
source: In contrast, Cas12a uses a single active site to make staggered cuts distant from the PAM, and the same active site can cleave free single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) non-specifically once the enzyme has been activated by specific target binding (Figure 1B; Zetsche et al., 2015; Swarts et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations to previous literature.

claim: The position of the 20-nucleotide spacer sequence in Cas12a crRNAs is opposite to that in Cas9 crRNAs.
source: Additionally, the position of the 20-nucleotide spacer sequence in Cas12a crRNAs is opposite to that in Cas9 crRNAs (3′ end versus 5′ end, respectively) (Zetsche et al., 2015; Deltcheva et al., 2011), and consequently, R-loop formation by each enzyme family occurs with opposing directionality (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations to previous literature.

claim: R-loop formation by Cas12a and Cas9 occurs with opposing directionality.
source: Additionally, the position of the 20-nucleotide spacer sequence in Cas12a crRNAs is opposite to that in Cas9 crRNAs (3′ end versus 5′ end, respectively) (Zetsche et al., 2015; Deltcheva et al., 2011), and consequently, R-loop formation by each enzyme family occurs with opposing directionality (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations to previous literature.

claim: Cas12a belongs to the type V family of CRISPR effector proteins, defined by the presence of a single RuvC DNase domain.
source: Cas12a belongs to the type V family of CRISPR effector proteins (whose names each begin with 'Cas12'), a classification defined by the presence of a single RuvC DNase domain (Koonin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: All Cas12 interference complexes share a spacer-3′ crRNA architecture.
source: Notably, although this classification is not strictly phylogenetic—the 'family' is actually a paraphyletic assembly of several evolutionarily independent protein lineages (Koonin et al., 2017; Makarova et al., 2020)—a second shared feature of all Cas12 interference complexes is the previously mentioned spacer-3′ crRNA architecture.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The RuvC domain of Cas12a exhibits stringent specificity for single-stranded substrates when activated for cleavage of free DNA in trans.
source: The RuvC domain of Cas12a exhibits stringent specificity for single-stranded substrates when activated for cleavage of free DNA in trans (Appendix 1) (Chen et al., 2018), suggesting that substrates cleaved in cis (i.e., the two DNA strands of a protein-bound R-loop) are also single-stranded during each of their respective cleavage events.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Non-target-strand cleavage is a prerequisite of DNA target-strand cutting by Cas12a.
source: This conformation likely permits initial non-target-strand cleavage, which is a prerequisite of DNA target-strand (TS) cutting (Figure 1B; Swarts and Jinek, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: In crystal structures of Cas12a-bound R-loops, the target-strand cleavage site is located within an ordered DNA duplex outside the R-loop, approximately 25 Å away from the RuvC active site.
source: However, in these same crystal structures, the target-strand cleavage site is located within an ordered DNA duplex outside the R-loop,~25 Å away from the RuvC active site and inverted with respect to the most probable catalytic orientation (Figure 1A; Swarts et al., 2017; Swarts and Jinek, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Cas12a binding to DNA distorts the target-strand cleavage site.
source: We suspected that dsDNA substrates of Cas12a would need to access a bent conformation to undergo target-strand cleavage.
evidence: This is the hypothesis stated at the beginning of the Results section, which is then tested experimentally.

claim: Permanganate selectively oxidizes thymines in non-B-form DNA structures.
source: In this assay, permanganate selectively oxidizes thymines in non-B-form (e.g., locally melted or otherwise distorted) DNA structures, and oxidized positions are subsequently identified through piperidine-catalyzed strand cleavage (which occurs specifically at thymidine glycols) and denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) (Figure 2A; Bui et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation describing the permanganate footprinting method.

claim: Thymines within the non-target strand displaced by the crRNA were heavily oxidized in permanganate assays.
source: Consistent with previous applications of the permanganate assay to CRISPR-Cas-generated R-loops (Xiao et al., 2017), thymines within the portion of the non-target strand displaced by the crRNA were heavily oxidized, reflecting the single-strandedness of this DNA tract (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2A showing the experimental data.

claim: Significant oxidation was observed at a thymine near the target-strand cleavage site in dCas12a-generated R-loops.
source: Interestingly, we also observed significant oxidation at a thymine near the target-strand cleavage site (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2A showing the experimental data.

claim: Cas12a binding promotes distortion of DNA in the PAM-distal flank of the R-loop.
source: At each step, we observed an increase in permanganate reactivity on both strands of the DNA that persisted seven base pairs past the end of the crRNA, suggesting that Cas12a binding promotes distortion of DNA in the PAM-distal flank of the R-loop (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2B showing the experimental data.

claim: Permanganate reactivity in the R-loop flank decreased with distance from the R-loop edge.
source: Additionally, permanganate reactivity decreased with distance from the R-loop edge (Figure 2B), consistent with NTS:TS fraying events that initiate from the R-loop edge (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2B showing the experimental data.

claim: The R-loop flank populates highly distorted, and probably unpaired, conformations when bound to Cas12a in solution.
source: Thus, while the R-loop flank has the potential for complete base pairing, this DNA tract populates highly distorted, and probably unpaired, conformations when bound to Cas12a in solution.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on permanganate reactivity data.

claim: A change in the location of duplex instability changes which phosphodiester bonds in the target strand are cleaved by the RuvC DNase.
source: A prediction of this model is that a change in the location of duplex instability should also change which phosphodiester bonds in the target strand are cleaved by the RuvC DNase.
evidence: This is a prediction stated in the Results section that is then tested experimentally.

claim: The A/T tract was highly reactive in the full R-loop but had limited reactivity in the truncated R-loop.
source: By implementing the permanganate assay on these complexes, we found that the A/T tract was highly reactive in the full R-loop but had limited reactivity in the truncated R-loop, suggesting that the distorted region had migrated with the edge of the R-loop (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3A showing the experimental data.

claim: As the R-loop edge was shifted toward the PAM, the target-strand cut-site distribution shifted toward the new R-loop edge.
source: As the R-loop edge was shifted toward the PAM, the target-strand cut-site distribution shifted toward the new R-loop edge (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3B showing the experimental data.

claim: When compensatory mutations were made in the crRNA to restore the original R-loop size, the target-strand cut sites moved back toward their original distribution.
source: When compensatory mutations were made in the crRNA to restore the original R-loop size, the target-strand cut sites moved back toward their original distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 5 showing the experimental data.

claim: The non-target-strand cut-site distribution did not change markedly as the R-loop was truncated.
source: Notably, the non-target-strand cut-site distribution did not change markedly as the R-loop was truncated, suggesting that non-target-strand cleavage is unrelated to nucleotide unpairing in the R-loop flank (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 6 showing the experimental data.

claim: The site of Cas12a-mediated target-strand cleavage is tied to the location of weakened base pairing.
source: These results imply that the site of Cas12a-mediated target-strand cleavage is tied to, and perhaps dictated by, the location of weakened base pairing.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the cut-site distribution experiments.

claim: Of three DNA targets that differed only in the sequence of their R-loop flank, the GC-rich substrate was cleaved most PAM-proximally.
source: In agreement with this prediction, of three DNA targets that differed only in the sequence of their R-loop flank—native protospacer, AT-rich, or GC-rich—the GC-rich substrate was cleaved most PAM-proximally (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3C showing the experimental data.

claim: Eliminating NTS:TS base pairing at positions 21–23 led to fast and PAM-distally shifted cleavage of the target strand.
source: Additionally, eliminating NTS:TS base pairing at positions 21–23 led to fast and PAM-distally shifted cleavage of the target strand in all cases (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 7 showing the experimental data.

claim: DNA distortion in the R-loop flank is an important enabler of Cas12a-catalyzed target-strand cleavage.
source: Together, these results suggest that DNA distortion in the R-loop flank is an important enabler of Cas12a-catalyzed target-strand cleavage.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the experimental data.

claim: The A/T tract in a protein-free R-loop mimic was slightly more reactive to permanganate than in the Cas12a-generated R-loop.
source: When we probed the permanganate reactivity of this protein-free R-loop, we found that the A/T tract was slightly more reactive than in the Cas12a-generated R-loop experiment (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4A showing the experimental data.

claim: Distortion of the R-loop flank is a phenomenon intrinsic to the R-loop boundary itself.
source: This result indicates that distortion of the R-loop flank is a phenomenon intrinsic to the R-loop boundary itself and that the protein only needs to hold the R-loop open to promote flexibility in the adjacent DNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the protein-free R-loop mimic experiments.

claim: The PAM-distal flank of the Cas9 R-loop experienced nearly background oxidation levels both in the protein-bound R-loop and in the protein-free mimic.
source: Remarkably, we found that the flank experienced nearly background oxidation levels both in the protein-bound R-loop (with dCas9 at a saturating concentration, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and in the protein-free mimic, suggesting that unlike 3′ R-loop flanks, 5′ R-loop flanks are not naturally unstable (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing the experimental data.

claim: An RNA:DNA hybrid can either stabilize or destabilize a juxtaposed DNA:DNA duplex terminus, depending on whether the hybrid terminus contains a 5′ RNA end or a 3′ RNA end.
source: Thus, an RNA:DNA hybrid can either stabilize or destabilize a juxtaposed DNA:DNA duplex terminus, depending on whether the hybrid terminus contains a 5′ RNA end or a 3′ RNA end, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the permanganate reactivity experiments comparing 3′ and 5′ R-loop flanks.

claim: There is a fundamental energetic difference in the conformational landscapes of 3′ versus 5′ R-loop flanks.
source: These results suggest a fundamental energetic difference in the conformational landscapes of 3′ versus 5′ R-loop flanks (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the permanganate reactivity experiments.

claim: The conformational difference between 3′ and 5′ R-loop flanks is intrinsic to strand polarity.
source: The conformational difference between 3′ and 5′ R-loop flanks is intrinsic to strand polarity, as the trends in permanganate reactivity were robust to changes in nucleic acid sequence, end chemistry, and non-target-strand cleavage state (Figure 4—figure supplements 3–6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to multiple supplementary figures showing the experimental data.

claim: The RNA-5′ dumbbell had a melting temperature 9°C higher than that of the RNA-3′ dumbbell.
source: Through temperature-dependent hyperchromicity measurements, we determined that the RNA-5′ dumbbell (resembling the PAM-distal R-loop edge of Cas9) had a melting temperature 9°C higher than that of the RNA-3′ dumbbell (resembling the PAM-distal R-loop edge of Cas12a) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5A showing the experimental data.

claim: The 3′ R-loop junctions frequently unstacked over the course of molecular dynamics simulations, while the 5′ R-loop junctions remained relatively stable.
source: Strikingly, the 3′ R-loop junctions frequently unstacked over the course of these short simulations, while the 5′ R-loop junctions remained relatively stable (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 5B showing the simulation data.

claim: The experimentally observed instability of 3′ R-loop flanks may arise from frequent unstacking events that comprise an early step in the DNA bending pathway.
source: Observation of large-scale conformational transitions relevant to Cas12a-mediated DNA cleavage, such as fraying or bending events, would likely require much longer simulations (Leroy et al., 1988), but these short simulations suggest that the experimentally observed instability of 3′ R-loop flanks may arise from frequent unstacking events that comprise an early step in the DNA bending pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The ability of the Cas12a RuvC active site to capture the target strand may rely on the active site's proximity to the uniquely malleable 3′ R-loop flank.
source: Specifically, the ability of the Cas12a RuvC active site to capture the target strand may rely on the active site's proximity to the uniquely malleable 3′ R-loop flank, which relies in turn upon the topology of the Cas12a R-loop (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: All known DNA-targeting Cas12 enzymes form R-loops of the topology that allows target-strand cleavage within a PAM-distal 3′ R-loop flank.
source: Intriguingly, all known DNA-targeting Cas12 enzymes, which are taxonomically defined by their minimal enzymatic machinery (a single RuvC DNase domain), form R-loops of the topology that allows target-strand cleavage within a PAM-distal 3′ R-loop flank (Yang et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2019; Karvelis et al., 2020) (for target-strand cleavage properties of Cas12i, see Appendix 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The universal type V R-loop topology may be the product of biophysically imposed selective pressures.
source: Given the importance of DNA bending in enabling a single RuvC active site to form double-strand breaks, we propose that the universal type V R-loop topology may be the product of biophysically imposed selective pressures.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: Under strong evolutionary pressure for immune responses that efficiently produce double-strand breaks, ancestral enzymes with PAM-distal 3′ R-loop flanks may have outperformed topology-inverted variants.
source: We hypothesize that, under the strong evolutionary pressure for immune responses that efficiently produce double-strand breaks (Heitman et al., 1999), ancestral enzymes with PAM-distal 3′ R-loop flanks outperformed topology-inverted variants, perhaps leading to the modern ubiquity of the Cas12a-like R-loop architecture in type V enzymes.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The extant diversity of Cas12 proteins likely did not emerge from a single CRISPR-associated ancestor but rather from many distinct transposon-encoded TnpB proteins.
source: Importantly, the extant diversity of Cas12 proteins likely did not emerge from a single CRISPR-associated ancestor but rather from many distinct transposon-encoded TnpB proteins (Koonin et al., 2017; Makarova et al., 2020), suggesting that several independent evolutionary trajectories have converged on the same R-loop topology.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Engineering a type V CRISPR nickase that performs fast non-target-strand cleavage but undetectable target-strand cleavage will likely require modifications that shield or distance the RuvC active site from the intrinsically labile 3′ R-loop flank.
source: Our permanganate reactivity results revealed that target-strand distortion in Cas12a-generated R-loops, as probed by our experimental techniques, can be explained by conformational dynamics intrinsic to the nucleic acids (Figure 4A). Thus, engineering a type V CRISPR nickase that performs fast non-target-strand cleavage but undetectable target-strand cleavage will likely require modifications that shield or distance the RuvC active site from the intrinsically labile 3′ R-loop flank.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: Placing a DNase domain near a 3′ R-loop flank would encourage fast target-strand cleavage.
source: Our results suggest that placing a DNase domain near a 3′ R-loop flank would encourage fast target-strand cleavage (for applications requiring double-strand breaks), while placing one near a 5′ R-loop flank would likely inhibit target-strand cleavage (for nickase applications).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: Placing a DNase domain near a 5′ R-loop flank would likely inhibit target-strand cleavage.
source: Our results suggest that placing a DNase domain near a 3′ R-loop flank would encourage fast target-strand cleavage (for applications requiring double-strand breaks), while placing one near a 5′ R-loop flank would likely inhibit target-strand cleavage (for nickase applications).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: The crystal structure shown in Figure 1A is from Francisella novicida Cas12a (FnCas12a, PDB 6I1K).
source: Crystal structure of the DNA-bound Cas12a interference complex from Francisella novicida (FnCas12a, PDB 61IK) (Swarts and Jinek, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend.

claim: The protein ortholog used for most experiments in this manuscript is from Acidaminoccus species (AsCas12a), which has approximately 40% identity to FnCas12a.
source: While the protein ortholog used for most experiments in this manuscript is from Acidaminoccus species (AsCas12a,~40% identity to FnCas12a), the FnCas12a crystal structure shown here represents the most complete structure of such a complex to date, most notably with respect to the DNA at the target-strand cleavage sites.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend.

claim: The FnCas12a crystal structure represents the most complete structure of a Cas12a-DNA complex to date, particularly with respect to the DNA at the target-strand cleavage sites.
source: While the protein ortholog used for most experiments in this manuscript is from Acidaminoccus species (AsCas12a,~40% identity to FnCas12a), the FnCas12a crystal structure shown here represents the most complete structure of such a complex to date, most notably with respect to the DNA at the target-strand cleavage sites.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend.

claim: Successful R-loop formation by Cas12a results in activation of the RuvC DNase active site to cleave three classes of DNA substrates: the non-target strand (in cis), the target strand (in cis), and non-specific ssDNA (in trans).
source: For Cas12a, successful R-loop formation results in activation of the RuvC DNase active site to cleave three classes of DNA substrates (yellow scissors): the non-target strand (in cis), the target strand (in cis), and non-specific ssDNA (in trans).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend.

claim: Cas9 contains two DNase domains: the RuvC domain cleaves the non-target strand, and the HNH domain cleaves the target strand.
source: Cas9 contains two DNase domains: the RuvC domain cleaves the non-target strand, and the HNH domain cleaves the target strand.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend.

claim: The affinity of dAsCas12a/crRNA for a cognate DNA target was assessed by an electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) and a filter-binding (FB) assay, yielding a KD of approximately 8 nM.
source: The affinity of dAsCas12a/crRNA for a cognate DNA target was assessed by an electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) and a filter-binding (FB) assay. dAsCas12a was titrated in a solution with fixed [crRNA] (750 nM) and [DNA probe] (100 pM), followed by separation of protein-bound DNA from free DNA. The EMSA indicated that the oligonucleotide annealing protocol yields 100% duplex DNA probe and that the binding conditions yield one major protein-bound species. 'Fraction bound' is defined as (background-subtracted volume of upper band)/(total background-subtracted lane volume) for the EMSA and (background-subtracted volume of Protran spot)/(total background-subtracted volume of Protran spot + Hybond N+ spot) for the filter-binding assay. The value of 'fraction bound' was 0 at [dAsCas12a]=0 for both assays (not shown in plot due to the logarithmic x-axis). When appropriate, data were fit to the sum of a hyperbola and a line (y = Bmax*x/(KD+x)+NS*x), where NS describes a non-specific binding mode. It is common to see Bmax values below 1 in EMSAs and filter-binding assays, in which the process of physical separation can disrupt bound species. KD for the EMSA was 8.2 nM (n = 1). KD for the filter-binding assay was 8.1 nM ±0.8 (SD) (n = 3).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 legend with experimental data.

claim: The KD of dAsCas12a for protospacer 2 (intact) was 54 nM ±12 (SD).
source: KD for protospacer 2 (intact) was 54 nM ±12 (SD) (n = 3).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 legend with experimental data.

claim: The KD of dAsCas12a for protospacer 2 (pre-gapped) was 2.8 nM ±0.5 (SD).
source: KD for protospacer 2 (pre-gapped) was 2.8 nM ±0.5 (SD) (n = 3).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 legend with experimental data.
